routes.label: Unit-value bound and an attaining load
Enumerate the number of five-pound rocks

officialSolution.label: 2018 AMC 12A
officialSolution.sourceTerms: The linked source retains its printed copyright notice and host terms. This project adds no copy of this PDF.

question: While exploring a cave, Carl comes across a collection of \(5\)-pound rocks worth \(\$14\) each, \(4\)-pound rocks worth \(\$11\) each, and \(1\)-pound rocks worth \(\$2\) each. There are at least \(20\) of each size. He can carry at most \(18\) pounds. What is the maximum value, in dollars, of the rocks he can carry out of the cave?
solution:
A 4-pound rock is worth \(11\) dollars, whereas four 1-pound rocks of the same total weight are worth only \(8\) dollars. Thus, once the number of 5-pound rocks is fixed, Carl should take as many 4-pound rocks as will fit, then fill the remaining capacity with 1-pound rocks.

There are enough 1-pound rocks to fill any unused capacity, so a maximum-value load weighs exactly \(18\) pounds. If \(a\) is the number of 5-pound rocks, then \(5a\le18\), giving exactly four cases: \(a=0,1,2,3\). The best load in each case is
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
\text{5-pound rocks}&\text{4-pound rocks}&\text{1-pound rocks}&\text{Value in dollars}\\
3&0&3&3(14)+3(2)=48\\
2&2&0&2(14)+2(11)=50\\
1&3&1&14+3(11)+2=49\\
0&4&2&4(11)+2(2)=48
\end{array}
\]
These cases cover every possible number of 5-pound rocks, and the replacement observation shows that no other load in any case is better. The maximum value is therefore \(\boxed{50}\) dollars, choice \(\text{C}\).
